# Design Specification: Cache Controller (cache_ctrl)

## 1. Overview

The cache controller manages a set-associative data cache. It accepts memory requests from the processor core, performs cache tag lookups, handles hits and misses, and controls access to the cache storage array. It also handles non-cacheable or bypass transactions and coordinates refill operations when a cache line must be fetched from memory.

The controller is parameterized for:

- number of cache ways,
- cache index width,
- tag width,
- cache line data width,
- cacheable address region boundary.

The cache line data width shall be 128 bits. The controller is only required to support this line width.

## 2. Reset and Initial State

On reset, the controller shall be idle and shall not have any outstanding memory request, refill, or cache write operation. All internal tracking state shall be cleared.

When idle, the controller shall be ready to accept a new memory request.

## 3. Request Acceptance

A memory request may be a read or a write. Each request provides:

- the cache index and tag portions of the addressed memory location,
- write data and byte enables for a write,
- transfer size,
- whether the operation is a read or a write,
- request qualifiers indicating validity and possible cancellation.

A new request is accepted only while no flush is blocking new operations and while the request has not been cancelled.

When the controller accepts a request, it shall tell the requester that the request has been granted. A request that is not granted shall not be considered accepted and must be presented again.

For a read, the grant may occur before the read data is available. The read data is returned separately when it is ready.

For a write, the grant shall be given only when the write has been safely handled, either by:

- updating the cache on a cacheable write hit,
- handing the write to the refill/miss path on a cacheable write miss,
- handing the write to the bypass path for a non-cacheable write.

## 4. Cacheable and Non-Cacheable Accesses

The controller shall distinguish between cacheable and non-cacheable addresses.

The boundary of the cacheable region is determined by the configured cache start address. Any address below that boundary shall be treated as non-cacheable.

Non-cacheable accesses shall use the bypass path. They shall not allocate a cache line, shall not update the cache data or status flags, and shall not be allowed to hit in the cache.

If the global bypass input is asserted, every access shall be treated as non-cacheable.

## 5. Cache Hit Behavior

A cache hit occurs when one of the ways in the selected cache set has a tag matching the request address and the line is valid.

### 5.1 Read Hit

On a read hit, the controller shall return the addressed 64-bit word from the selected cache line.

The read completion shall be indicated to the requester at the same time the read data is presented.

### 5.2 Write Hit

On a write hit, the controller shall update the addressed 64-bit word in the selected cache line. Only the byte lanes selected by the request byte enables shall be modified; all other bytes in the line shall remain unchanged.

The updated cache line shall be marked valid and dirty.

A write hit shall not be granted to the requester until the cache storage has accepted the write.

## 6. Cache Miss Behavior

A cache miss occurs when no way in the selected cache set has a matching valid tag.

### 6.1 Read Miss

On a read miss, the controller shall issue a refill request for the missing cache line.

The controller shall wait for the refill path to provide the requested critical word. When the critical word becomes available, the controller shall return it as the read data and complete the read.

The rest of the cache line may continue to be filled after the critical word has been returned.

### 6.2 Write Miss

On a write miss, the controller shall issue a refill request that includes the write data and byte enables of the store.

The write shall be considered complete when the refill/miss path accepts the write request. The controller need not wait for the full cache line refill before granting the write.

## 7. Outstanding Miss Aliasing

The controller shall check whether a miss request for the same cache line is already outstanding.

If an outstanding miss matches the current request’s line, the controller shall not issue a duplicate miss request. It shall instead wait for the outstanding miss to be resolved, then perform another cache lookup and complete the request based on the updated cache state.

This behavior applies to both reads and writes. A write that aliases an outstanding miss shall not be granted until it can be completed from the updated cache or through its own miss path.

## 8. Bypass / Non-Cacheable Data Path

For non-cacheable accesses, the controller shall forward the request to the bypass path.

A bypass read shall return data from the bypass response. The returned data shall be presented to the requester as the read result.

A bypass write shall be forwarded with its write data and byte enables. It shall not update the cache.

## 9. Interaction with New Requests

The controller may accept a new request while an existing request is being completed, provided the cache storage is available and the new request is not blocked.

If a new request is presented while the current request is completing and the cache storage cannot accept the new access, the new request shall not be granted. The controller shall return to idle, and the requester must present the new request again.

The controller shall not start a new request while a flush is active.

## 10. Flush and Cancel Behavior

### 10.1 Flush

A flush shall prevent the controller from starting new memory requests. Operations already in progress may continue until they complete, but no new operation shall be initiated due to the flush.

### 10.2 Request Cancellation

If a request is cancelled, the controller shall abort any processing of that request and return to idle.



The controller shall provide a completion indication for the cancelled transaction so that the requesting pipeline no longer waits for data.

## 11. Busy Indication

The controller shall provide a busy status whenever it is not idle.

The busy status indicates that the controller is currently handling one or more operations. It does not itself prevent a new request from being presented; the request grant mechanism determines whether a new access is accepted.

## 12. Cache Storage Access Behavior

The controller shall address the cache storage using the index of the current request.

For a tag lookup, the controller shall request access to all ways of the selected set and observe which way, if any, matches the tag.

For a write on a store hit, the controller shall request access only to the matching way.

The controller shall not update any cache way on a hit read or on a non-cacheable access.

## 13. Summary of Required Behaviors

- Provide idle state after reset and after completion of all operations.
- Accept and grant reads and writes according to the cacheable/bypass classification.
- Return read data for cache hits, cache misses, and non-cacheable reads.
- Update the cache correctly on write hits and preserve unmodified bytes.
- Issue miss requests for cacheable misses.
- Avoid duplicate miss requests for the same cache line.
- Forward non-cacheable accesses to the bypass path.
- Halt new request initiation on flush.
- Abort cleanly on request cancellation.
- Keep the requester informed through grant and read-data completion indications.

# Scoreboard Behavioral Specification

## 1. Purpose

The scoreboard tracks instructions that have been accepted for execution but have not yet been retired/committed. It preserves program order for issue and commit while allowing write-back/completion to occur out of order. It also provides register-clobber information and operand-forwarding behavior for source registers.

The module shall:

- accept decoded instructions in order,
- assign each accepted instruction a unique tracking identifier,
- track completion of each in-flight instruction using write-back information,
- expose the oldest tracked instruction for commit, and
- provide information about pending register writes and forwarded operand values.

## 2. Configuration

The module is configured with:

- the number of tracked instruction entries, and
- the number of independent write-back ports.

The number of entries must be a power of two. The practical number of outstanding in-flight instructions is one less than the configured number of entries. All write-back ports may carry completions in the same cycle.

The tracking identifier used to associate a write-back with an instruction must be wide enough to address every configured entry.

## 3. Reset and Flush

On reset, the module shall start empty:

- no instructions are tracked,
- no registers are reported as clobbered,
- no operand-forwarding values are valid,
- the issue and commit positions are reset to the beginning.

A flush shall have the same effect: all in-flight instructions are discarded and the module returns to the empty state. A flush shall take precedence over any simultaneous issue, commit, or write-back. A write-back that arrives in the same cycle as a flush shall be ignored because its target instruction is no longer active.

## 4. Instruction Issue and Tracking

The module receives at most one decoded instruction per cycle.

A decoded instruction shall be accepted only when:

- the module is not full,
- no unresolved branch is currently preventing issue, and
- the issue consumer acknowledges acceptance.

When accepted, the instruction becomes an in-flight tracked instruction. It shall be assigned a tracking identifier. The same identifier shall be presented with the instruction to the execution side and later used by the write-back interface to target the correct entry.

The module shall not accept a new instruction when it is full. The maximum number of outstanding instructions is one less than the configured entry count.

While an unresolved branch condition is active, the module shall not allow a new instruction to be issued. Instructions already in flight are not affected by this condition.

If a decoded instruction is not accepted in a cycle, it shall remain available and be presented again in a subsequent cycle.

Instruction issue shall be in order. The relative order of accepted instructions shall be preserved until commit.

## 5. Write-Back and Completion

Each write-back port may present a completing instruction in any order. The write-back is associated with one of the tracked instructions by its tracking identifier.

On a valid write-back:

- if the identified instruction is still active, the module shall record that the instruction has completed,
- the returned result data shall be stored,
- if the write-back carries an exception, that exception information shall be stored with the instruction, and
- the entry shall be marked ready for commit.

A write-back targeting an instruction that is no longer active, such as after a flush or after commit, shall be ignored.

Multiple write-backs per cycle shall be supported up to the configured number of write-back ports. Concurrent write-backs in the same cycle shall refer to distinct tracked instructions.

Write-back acceptance shall not be blocked by issue back-pressure, by a full scoreboard, or by an unresolved branch condition.

Completion may occur out of order. The module shall use the tracking identifier, not the completion order, to associate the write-back with the correct instruction.

## 6. Commit

The module shall continuously present the oldest tracked instruction on the commit interface. This presentation includes the instruction’s result data, exception information, destination register, and completion status.

When a commit acknowledge is received, the module shall retire that instruction and remove it from the tracked set. After retirement, the next-oldest instruction shall become visible for commit.

The commit acknowledge shall be used only when the presented instruction is already marked complete.

If the retired instruction carries an exception, the exception information shall be visible to the commit consumer before the instruction is retired.

Commit shall occur in program order. An older instruction must be retired before a younger instruction can be retired.

## 7. Operand Read and Forwarding

The module provides two independent source-operand read interfaces.

For each requested source register:

- if the source register is architectural register 0, the returned value must be zero and the valid indication must be false;
- if an in-flight instruction targets that register and has already completed, the stored result shall be returned and marked valid;
- if an in-flight instruction targets that register but has not yet completed, the valid indication shall be false;
- if no in-flight instruction targets that register, the module shall not provide a forwarded value;
- if a write-back for that register is presented in the same cycle, and the write-back does not carry an exception, the incoming write-back data shall be returned and marked valid, taking priority over previously stored data.

A write-back that carries an exception shall not be used for same-cycle operand forwarding.

## 8. Register Clobber Indication

For each architectural destination register, the module shall indicate whether an in-flight instruction will eventually write that register.

For every non-zero architectural register:

- if at least one tracked, not-yet-committed instruction targets that register, the module shall indicate which functional unit will produce the result;
- otherwise, the module shall indicate that no functional unit will write that register.

Architectural register 0 shall always be reported as not clobbered.

This information shall reflect all currently tracked instructions that have not yet committed, including those that have already completed but are waiting to commit.

## 9. Ordering and Consistency Requirements

The module shall preserve the following ordering behavior:

- instructions are issued in program order,
- instructions are committed in program order,
- instructions may complete out of order,
- the tracking identifier assigned at issue is unique among active instructions,
- the oldest tracked instruction is always the one presented for commit.

The module assumes that the surrounding issue logic prevents multiple in-flight instructions from writing the same architectural destination register, so the clobber and forwarding outputs remain unambiguous. It also assumes that no two write-back ports present the same tracking identifier in the same cycle.
